memory_update.text: DNB should remain in the Layer 1 universe as a direct supplier-risk intelligence candidate; key gating evidence is energy/utility/industrial customer exposure and product revenue traction.

ULS should remain in the Layer 1 universe as a TIC/certification chokepoint candidate for energy storage, renewables, grid-code compliance, utility product certification, and power-generation equipment.
WCC should remain in the Layer 1 universe as an underfollowed electrical/utility distribution and procurement-services candidate tied to constrained energy infrastructure equipment.

Moody's supplied evidence supports the core node hypothesis: energy supplier risk may be becoming structural rather than episodic, increasing the relevance of risk analytics, TIC, procurement platforms, and specialty distributors.

MRC is a plausible small-cap distributor coverage-gap candidate for a later pass focused on energy, gas-utility, PVF, valve, and infrastructure distribution, but was not included in the capped four-name list because this pass prioritized broader supplier-risk intelligence, TIC, and electrical procurement exposure.
ULS should be tracked as an underfollowed public TIC gatekeeper for grid, storage, inverter, renewable, transformer and switchgear qualification rather than as a conventional energy stock.
DNOW replaces MRC in the current public universe after the November 2025 DNOW-MRC merger; map DNOW as a low-attention energy/industrial supply-chain assurance and specialty distribution candidate.
The node has two investable sublanes: data/risk platforms such as MCO, and physical procurement-assurance/distribution layers such as WCC and DNOW.
Need deeper evidence on energy-specific revenue contribution for MCO and ULS and scarcity-driven margin/backlog evidence for WCC and DNOW before these candidates can advance beyond Layer 1.

Pure-play supplier-risk intelligence is hard to express through US-listed equities after Dun & Bradstreet was taken private in August 2025; many procurement and supply-chain-risk platforms appear private or buried inside diversified software/data companies.

ULS should remain in the underfollowed lane for energy because its testing/certification role touches batteries, storage, grid-code compliance, transformers, switchgear, renewables, and utility equipment; verify energy-specific revenue growth before later-layer promotion.

WCC maps to the node as a utility/electrical distributor and supply-chain-services provider; verify whether constrained grid equipment, data-center power, utility customers, and contractor demand are material enough to drive incremental earnings.

DNOW is the most energy-specific small/mid-cap candidate found in this pass, with supply-chain services, digital procurement, PVF/pumps/equipment distribution, gas utility, downstream, energy evolution, and industrial exposure.

For this node, the chokepoint is likely less about owning scarce physical equipment and more about qualification, availability, procurement workflow, inventory visibility, supplier networks, and project-critical distribution reliability.
WCC should be tracked as a reference/anchor for energy procurement and utility distribution; verify whether constrained electrical equipment increases revenue visibility or margins.
DNB is an underfollowed supplier-risk intelligence candidate; direct energy exposure is plausible but unproven and needs customer/use-case evidence.
ULS is a strong underfollowed TIC candidate for grid-code compliance, inverter/BESS certification, and energy equipment market access.
MG is a speculative-shadow small-cap for energy infrastructure inspection and asset integrity; keep only if power-generation or grid-related inspection growth is confirmed.
Need a follow-up pass on non-US-listed TIC leaders and ADR/OTC mappings such as SGS, Bureau Veritas, Intertek, and DNV/private peers to benchmark ULS and MG.

node: Energy supplier-risk intelligence, procurement analytics, inspection, certification, and supply-chain assurance
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Layer 1B expands the public-company universe for the supplier-risk assurance node in energy. The reference lane is Moody's because the supplied evidence directly frames energy supplier risk as becoming structural rather than episodic. The underfollowed lane emphasizes public companies that are not normally classified as energy beneficiaries but may benefit if utilities, EPCs, developers, industrial buyers, and energy infrastructure operators spend more on supplier visibility, qualification, certification, and constrained-equipment procurement. No buy/sell view is implied. Expanded the universe for the supplier-risk intelligence/procurement-assurance node. The cleanest public mappings are not pure-play energy companies: Moody's is the reference data/risk platform; UL Solutions is a listed testing/certification gatekeeper for grid, storage, inverter, renewables and utility equipment; WESCO is a large electrical/utility distributor and supply-chain services provider; DNOW is a smaller, more energy-specific distributor with PVF, engineered equipment, digital commerce and supply-chain services across upstream, midstream, gas utilities, downstream, energy transition and industrial markets. D&B would have been relevant but is excluded because it was taken private in August 2025. Layer 1B expands a non-obvious energy supply-chain assurance node. The strongest public-market mappings are not pure supplier-risk-intelligence software names, because several obvious platforms are private or have been taken private. The investable lane therefore shifts toward testing/certification gates,
